newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Suharto's son denies interest in Astra.
newsitem.headline: Suharto's son denies interest in Astra.

text.p: Indonesian President Suharto's youngest son denied on Thursday that he was interested in purchasing a stake in automobile conglomerate PT Astra International.

"It's not true. We don't need Astra to develop Mobnas (the national car)," said Hutomo Mandala Putra, whose PT Timor Putra Nasional has been awarded the only licence to produce Indonesia's national car.
Astra shares surged last month on a wave of buying and brokers said a takeover bid could be in progress.
Tobacco tycoon Putera Sampoerna, the head of cigarette maker PT Hanjaya Mandala Sampoerna, later said he had bought a 9.81 percent stake in Astra on his individual account.
A PT Sampoerna subsidiary said it had bought an additional 2.85 percent stake in Astra, giving Putera Sampoerna effectively the biggest stake in the country's largest automobile manufacturer.

Brokers had named Mandala Putra as being one of those interested in Astra since he could use its wide production and distribution base for his Timor sedan. Some had said Putera Sampoerna could be prepared to sell his stake to Mandala Putra.
Mandala Putra said he did not need either Astra's manufacturing or dealership facilities as he already had better facilities.
"We have better and more efficient facilities than any other existing car manufacturer," he told reporters.
PT Timor Putra Nasional was given tax and tariff breaks under the controversial car policy earlier this year to manufacture a national car in cooperation with Kia Motors Corp. of South Korea.
The grant of the tax breaks is subject to meeting local content requirements in each year of operation, rising to 60 percent within three years.
But the government has allowed the company to import an initial batch of sedans duty-free from South Korea.
Japan has complained to the World Trade Organisation that the policy is unfair while the United States and the European Union have said they will follow suit.

The tax breaks allow the Timor sedan to be sold at about half the price of comparable sedans and existing automobile joint ventures in Indonesia, most of which have Japanese partners, have said their sales will be badly hit.
